answers.working:
**Squamous epithelium** is a single layer of thin, flat cells (as in the walls of blood vessels and the air sacs of the lungs). Being so thin, it serves as a **diffusion barrier**, so P matches (iv).

**Cuboidal epithelium** has cube-shaped cells with a round nucleus in the centre of the cell. It lines ducts of glands and kidney tubules, where it carries out secretion and absorption, so Q matches (iii).

**Columnar epithelium** has tall cells whose nuclei sit at the base of the cell. It lines the stomach and intestine and also works in secretion and absorption, so R matches (ii).

**Ciliated epithelium** is columnar or cuboidal epithelium carrying cilia, with basal nuclei. The beating cilia move particles and mucus in one direction (as in the bronchioles and fallopian tubes), so S matches (i).

So the matching is P - (iv), Q - (iii), R - (ii), S - (i). So the answer is option (C).

In the stomach, the inactive **pepsinogen** (a zymogen) is converted by HCl into the active enzyme **pepsin**. Pepsin breaks proteins down into **proteoses and peptones**, which are partially digested proteins.

Options (A) and (B) describe pepsinogen and pepsin themselves, not their product. Option (C) describes the alkaline fluid of the intestine, not peptones.

answers.working:
**Insulin** is a protein made of two polypeptide chains built from many different amino acids. A chain of different monomers is a **heteropolymer**, so P matches (iv).

**Inulin** is a polysaccharide made of fructose units only. A chain of one kind of monomer is a **homopolymer**, so Q matches (ii).

**Lectins** (such as concanavalin A) are listed among plant **secondary metabolites**, so R matches (i).

**Lecithin** is phosphatidylcholine, a phospholipid whose head group is choline. Choline carries a nitrogen bonded to four carbon groups, which makes it a **quaternary ammonium** derivative, so S matches (iii).

Note the look-alike pairs: insulin (protein) versus inulin (fructose polymer), and lectin (protein) versus lecithin (lipid).

So the answer is option (A).

answers.label: A
answers.working:
The mitotic spindle is made of **microtubules**. The assembly of the spindle begins in **prophase**: the centrosomes move to opposite poles and send out the microtubules (asters and spindle fibres) that will later attach to the chromosomes.

A drug that stops microtubule formation therefore acts first on this prophase event. Because no spindle forms, the chromosomes can also not line up at the metaphase plate or be pulled apart in anaphase, so the cell is held at that point (this is why colchicine-treated cells are seen stuck at metaphase). But the earliest stage whose events need microtubules, and so the first to be affected, is prophase.

So the answer is option (A).
answers.flag: Wording-dependent: spindle assembly starts in prophase (A, chosen), but the classic textbook effect of microtubule poisons such as colchicine is arrest at metaphase (D). 'First to get affected' points to prophase; a setter thinking of colchicine arrest may have intended metaphase.

answers.value: In monocot seeds, the membraneous seed coat that is fused with the fruit wall is called the aleurone layer.
answers.working:
Check each statement.

(A) is correct: in many dicots such as bean, gram and pea the endosperm is used up as the seed matures, so the mature seed has no endosperm (non-endospermic seeds).

(B) is correct: the dicot seed coat has two layers, the outer **testa** and the inner **tegmen**.

(C) is incorrect: in a monocot seed such as maize, the membranous seed coat is fused with the fruit wall, but it is not called the aleurone layer. The **aleurone layer** is the protein-rich outer layer of the endosperm that separates it from the embryo.

(D) is correct: the plumule and radicle of a monocot embryo are enclosed in sheaths called the **coleoptile** and **coleorhiza**.

So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: A
answers.working:
In temperate climates the cambium is very active in spring and forms wide, light-coloured xylem with large vessels: **spring wood** (early wood). In autumn it is less active and forms narrow, dark, dense xylem: **autumn wood** (late wood).

One band of spring wood plus one band of autumn wood forms an **annual ring**, one for each year of growth. Counting these rings gives the age of the tree.

Heart wood and sap wood only describe the inner dead, darker wood and the outer living, lighter wood; they do not record years. So the answer is option (A).

answers.value: The catalytic redox center of Nitrogenase contains Mo and Fe as cofactors.
answers.working:
(A) is correct: **nitrogenase** is a Mo-Fe protein. Its catalytic redox centre (the iron-molybdenum cofactor) contains molybdenum and iron.

(B) is wrong: nitrogenase is highly sensitive to oxygen and needs **anaerobic** conditions. This is why root nodules contain leg-haemoglobin, which removes oxygen.

(C) is wrong: the amides asparagine and glutamine are formed from aspartic acid and glutamic acid by adding another amino group (not by transamination), and they are carried to other parts of the plant in the **xylem**, not the phloem.

(D) is wrong: nitrogenase reduces \(\mathrm{N_2}\) to ammonia, \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), not to nitrate.

So the answer is option (A).

answers.value: Variation in the potency and concentration of reserpine produced by Rauwolfia vomitoria.
answers.working:
**Genetic diversity** is the variation in genes within a single species. The standard example is the medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria: populations growing in different Himalayan ranges differ genetically, and this shows up as differences in the potency and concentration of the drug reserpine they make.

Option (B) compares numbers of plant species, and (D) compares numbers of amphibian species: both are **species diversity**. Option (C) compares the variety of ecosystems: that is **ecological diversity**.

So the answer is option (A).

No tRNA reads a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA). Instead, a protein called a **release factor** binds to the stop codon in the A site of the ribosome. This causes the finished polypeptide to be released and the ribosome to come apart.

The sigma factor and rho factor are proteins of **transcription** in bacteria (sigma helps start it, rho helps end it), not of translation. So the answer is option (C).

answers.working:
**Sertoli cells** in the seminiferous tubules provide nutrition to the developing sperm, so P matches (iv).

The **placenta** works as an endocrine organ and secretes hormones such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), so R matches (i).

The **urethra** carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside, so S matches (ii). (Carrying urine away from the kidney is the job of the ureter, so (iii) is not used.)

That leaves **follicle stimulating hormone** with (v), triggering ovulation. FSH and LH both peak in the middle of the menstrual cycle, and this mid-cycle hormone peak leads to ovulation.

Only one option has P - (iv), R - (i) and S - (ii): P - (iv), Q - (v), R - (i), S - (ii). So the answer is option (B).

Note: as printed, (v) is only loosely true of FSH. Strictly, it is the surge of LH that causes the Graafian follicle to rupture; FSH peaks alongside it.
answers.flag: Pairing Q (FSH) with (v) 'Triggers ovulation' is loose: NCERT credits the LH surge with inducing ovulation (FSH peaks at the same time). Still, B is the only option consistent with P, R and S.

answers.label: C
answers.working:
**Splicing** of hnRNA (removing introns and joining exons to make mature mRNA) happens only in **eukaryotes**. Bacterial genes have no introns, so bacteria do not splice their RNA.

Typhoid (Salmonella typhi), pertussis or whooping cough (Bordetella pertussis) and tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) are all caused by **bacteria**. Malaria is caused by **Plasmodium**, a eukaryotic protozoan, whose genes carry introns that must be spliced out.

So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: D
answers.working:
A **competitive inhibitor** looks like the substrate and binds to the **active site**, competing with the substrate for it. So we need the shapes that carry the substrate's shape (a downward-pointing triangle) and can fit the V-shaped active site.

**P** is an oval sitting on a downward triangle, and **S** is a diamond whose lower half is a downward triangle. Both can slot their triangle into the active site, so both are competitive inhibitors.

Q (square), R (square joined to a rounded piece) and T (overlapping circles) have no triangular part. Their square and rounded shapes match the allosteric sites instead, so they would act as allosteric (non-competitive) inhibitors.

So the answer is option (D).

answers.label: D
answers.working:
Sickle cell anaemia is recessive, so the affected people are homozygous recessive. Their frequency is \(q^2\):

\(q^2 = \dfrac{4}{10000} = 0.0004\), so \(q = 0.02\).

Then the normal allele frequency is \(p = 1 - q = 0.98\).

Under **Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium** the heterozygote frequency is \(2pq = 2 \times 0.98 \times 0.02 = 0.0392\).

Number of heterozygotes \(= 0.0392 \times 10000 = 392\).

(As a check, \(p^2 \times 10000 = 9604\) homozygous normal, and \(9604 + 392 + 4 = 10000\).) So the answer is option (D).

answers.value: Lane 1: bands at 1900, 1700, 500 and 400; Lane 2: bands at 1900, 1100, 900 and 600
answers.working:
The recombinant plasmid is \(3500 + 1000 = 4500\) bp. Mark the sites as positions around the circle, going clockwise and starting at the EcoR I site (position 0):

| Site | Position (bp) |
|---|---|
| EcoR I | 0 |
| Not I (in the insert, 400 bp from EcoR I) | 400 |
| Hind III (end of the 1000 bp insert) | 1000 |
| Not I (1100 bp clockwise from Hind III) | 2100 |
| Not I (500 bp anticlockwise from EcoR I) | 4000 |

**(a) Not I + EcoR I** cuts at 0, 400, 2100 and 4000. The pieces are \(400 - 0 = 400\), \(2100 - 400 = 1700\), \(4000 - 2100 = 1900\) and \(4500 - 4000 = 500\). Lane 1: 1900, 1700, 500 and 400 bp.

**(b) Not I + Hind III** cuts at 400, 1000, 2100 and 4000. The pieces are \(1000 - 400 = 600\), \(2100 - 1000 = 1100\), \(4000 - 2100 = 1900\) and \((4500 - 4000) + 400 = 900\). Lane 2: 1900, 1100, 900 and 600 bp.

In each lane the pieces add up to 4500 bp, as they must. Options (B) and (D) show a 900 bp band in lane 1, which ignores the Not I site inside the insert that splits it into 500 and 400. So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: C
answers.working:
Look at generation III: the daughter III-2 is affected, but both her parents, II-2 and II-3, are unaffected. A trait that appears in a child of two unaffected parents must be **recessive**, with both parents being carriers. This rules out autosomal dominant, option (D).

If the trait were **X-linked recessive**, an affected daughter would need the recessive allele on the X from her father too, so her father II-3 would have to be affected. He is unaffected, so the trait is not X-linked. The trait is therefore **autosomal recessive**.

For III-2 to be homozygous recessive (aa), she must receive one a from each parent. So II-3, although unaffected, must be **heterozygous (Aa)**. (II-2 is also Aa: she got the a from her affected father I-2.)

So the answer is option (C).
